claims.statement: Milgram published The Small-World Problem in Psychology Today 1967 vol1(1) pp61-67
The fictive international café acquaintance dialogue introducing the 1967 article is an illustration, not documented subject interview
claims.locator: 1967 paper opening anecdote without study protocol

claims.statement: Travers and Milgram technical report is Sociometry vol32(4) 425-443 in 1969
1969 study recruited 296 starter volunteers including 100 Nebraska stockholders, 96 other Nebraska volunteers and 100 Boston volunteers
Target was stockbroker living in Sharon Massachusetts and working in Boston; document passed only among first-name acquaintances
217 starters actually forwarded document and 64 chains completed
64/296=21.6 percent of all starters and 64/217=29.5 percent of starters who forwarded
Completed chains alone had mean 5.2 intermediaries and no universal all-pairs or shortest path inference follows
claims.locator: 1969 p425 Abstract and p432 completed chains

claims.statement: 16+10+5=31 of the 64 completed chains used three penultimate contacts, about 48 percent
1969 study distinguishes geographic and occupation-based routes with different chain length patterns
Uncompleted chains, volunteer sampling and single target prevent generalization to any human pair; missingness may bias success-only chain mean
1967 public essay and 1969 296-person technical report contain distinct early study descriptions; do not conflate Kansas pilot with later Nebraska Boston cohorts
Existence of short network paths differs from decentralized discovery and from participants continuing a real-world chain
claims.locator: 1969 paper procedure and conclusions plus graph-theoretic reasoning
